items.body: Idaho Conservation League Executive Director Courtney Washburn Experienced conservationist and policy leader Courtney Washburn has been named the new executive director of the Idaho Conservation League, the league and its board of directors announced last month. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Washburn succeeds previous Executive Director Justin Hayes, who announced last year he was taking a new position at the group American Rivers. The Idaho Conservation League is a more than 50-year-old nonprofit organization with a mission to protect clean air, clean water, land and wildlife. The new role represents a homecoming for Washburn, who previously served as the Idaho Conservation League’s community conservation director and statehouse lobbyist from 2006 to 2015. In her new role, Washburn is focusing on connecting and partnering with people and groups to take on the challenges of protecting Idaho. “I’m really focused on both growing the conservation community and connecting – or reconnecting, depending on how long people have lived in Idaho – with the conservation values and the actions that’s needed to protect this great state,” Washburn said in an interview Wednesday. “Progress would be to finally dispel the myth that people who care about conservation are associated with one party or another,” Washburn said. “I’d really like to see a durable kind of big tent. Everyone has a voice to speak up for their values, whether it be clean air, clean water, public lands.” “People care deeply about their state, and if you get to the core values, there are far less arguments, in my experience,” she added. Washburn also previously served as executive director for Conservation Voters for Idaho from 2015 to 2020. More recently, Washburn served as chief of staff for the city of Boise from 2020 to 2026, where she directed municipal operations, longterm planning and climate initiatives. Boise Dev reported in May that Boise Mayor Lauren McLean authorized a large severance payment for Washburn after Washburn left the city position. Data centers on public land represent a new challenge for water and wildlife habitat Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US While many of the conservation priorities around protecting clean water, clean air, land and wildlife have remained similar since Washburn’s first experience with the Idaho Conservation League, one new challenge has emerged recently. “Discussions about public lands, how they should be managed, who should own them and what should be developed on them are certainly bedrock conversations that have been happening in Idaho forever, but the new issue in that space is definitely data centers proposed on public lands,” Washburn said. Washburn said she opposes data centers on public lands and is working to study how they would affect water, wildlife, wildlife habitat, birds, energy use and infrastructure in Idaho. items.body: The Snake River runs through Idaho Falls. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho has periodically faced serious threats to its water sovereignty from an overreaching federal government. In the early 1950s, when Len Jordan was Idaho governor, the feds wanted to build a massive dam on the Snake River in Hells Canyon. That would have usurped Idaho control of its upstream waters. Jordan stopped the proposal, opting instead for the three existing Idaho Power company dams in order to protect Idaho’s control of those waters. The next water fight occurred after I was elected as Idaho attorney general in 1982. Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights Idaho Power had just received an erroneous decision from the Idaho Supreme Court, giving the company practical control of Snake River waters above its Swan Falls Dam in Ada County. Gov. John Evans and I were able to work together behind the scenes and across the political aisle to defeat that threat. When we were able to get the conflict settled to the state’s advantage, the next federal threat raised its ugly head. In December 1987, Congress was on the verge of approving legislation that would have given the feds the ability to control the flow of Snake River waters above Deer Flats Wildlife Refuge in Canyon County. The matter was being handled behind closed doors in congressional offices. When my staff members learned that a political deal was being made to compromise the state’s interests, I blew the whistle, the Idaho water community erupted in anger, and the threat was brought to a screeching halt. Anyone interested in the details can check out pages 337-345 of my book on the subject – “ A Little Dam Problem .” The latest threat to Idaho’s water sovereignty surfaced less than two months ago. Shortly after it was announced that the Idaho National Laboratory had been selected as a finalist for designation as a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus , the Trump administration launched an extremely troubling lawsuit challenging Idaho’s ability to “administer” the federal water right at the INL. In practical terms it means that, if there is a water shortage involving water rights in the INL vicinity, any reduction or mitigation would fall wholly upon the shoulders of other Idaho water users — farmers, fish producers and other folks dependent on those waters. The INL would be exempt. Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming ‘supremacy’ over our water is a gut punch to all Idahoans The lawsuit was filed against Idaho in the federal court in Boise on Sept. 11, without any attendant publicity from either side. While the allegations focus primarily upon the INL water right, the complaint seeks much broader relief. The Trump administration wants “a declaration that the Idaho Department of Water Resources lacks the authority to administer federal water rights” and “an order permanently enjoining the Director of IDWR from exercising his authority” under any state law as to the United States or its agencies. In short, the administration is asking the court to prevent Idaho from administering federal water rights anywhere within state borders. This is wholly without precedent and contrary to the determination of rights in the Snake River Basin Adjudication . The agreement settling the Swan Falls water right fight called for filing a case in state court to adjudicate all water rights to Snake River Basin waters. A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote
items.body: Volunteers pass boxes of signatures supporting a ballot initiative to end Idaho's strict ban on abortion on July 2, 2026, outside the state Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Oct. 30, 2026. A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote the ballot measure days before the election. In an opinion released late Friday night , Judge Davis VanderVelde found the ads did not violate Idaho campaign finance laws and declined to keep them from being broadcast by local stations. A Republican Party operative and three board members of Too Extreme for Idaho, which opposes restoring abortion rights under Prop 1, filed their lawsuit Tuesday morning . They said the scheme used by Idahoans United for Women and Families (IUWF), the Idaho Democratic Party and its gubernatorial candidate, Terri Pickens, concealed the true origin of who paid for the ads. IUWF, which qualified Prop 1 for the ballot, gave the Idaho Democratic Party more than $720,000 in recent weeks. The party then purchased advertising through Pickens’ campaign. All political candidates receive significant discounts on ads in the 60 days leading up to an election compared to political groups. “Ultimately, Plaintiffs’ assertion that the monies from IUWF were specifically contributed for support of Proposition 1 with the intent of concealing the original donor for such advertisements requires logical leaps that are not fully supported by the evidence,” VanderVelde wrote. Each of these transactions is publicly available in the state’s campaign finance database, which the plaintiffs cited in the evidence presented to the judge. VanderVelde said there’s also no evidence showing that IUWF still controlled the hundreds of thousands of dollars it donated to the state Democratic Party. An attorney for the defendants argued in court Thursday that the party had the final say in how any of that money was spent, which VanderVelde said was not proven otherwise by the plaintiffs. “The Court recognizes that the parties have had a short time to advance this lawsuit and that if there was additional time, additional facts may be developed by either party which could lend further credence to their claims or defenses,” he wrote. That said, the judge found there may still be outstanding legal questions about whether the ads are truly for a candidate or a proposition and whether the lower rates should apply. “However, without further law or authority significant questions remain as to what constitutes an appropriate advertisement under the law in order to qualify as an advertisement promoting a candidate.” Tom Luna, one of the plaintiffs, released a statement saying he and the three other men who brought the lawsuit disagree with the decision, but that it was important voters know who paid for the ads. “I’m sure many voters are as mad as I am about these dirty tricks. Let’s make sure we turn our frustration into action by showing up on Election Day, making our voices heard, and standing for life,” Luna said. A request for comment from the Idaho Democratic Party wasn’t immediately returned late Friday night. Memorandum Decision and Order Denying Motion For Prelimiary Injunction

items.body: The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals as photographed on June 12, 2017, in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) Update: This story was updated at 5:10 p.m. on Oct. 30 with a comment from the plaintiff, Dr. Stacy Seyb. A federal appeals court panel ruled on Friday that Idaho’s abortion ban may continue to be fully enforced, including against a Boise doctor who challenged the ban’s lack of health exemption. A U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit panel ruled 2-1 to continue to block a lower court’s decision that would have prevented prosecution of maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb if he performed abortions in which he determined there were serious risks to the mother’s health or mental health. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. Seyb’s challenge, which argued Idaho’s abortion ban’s lack of exemptions to prevent serious harm to the mother’s health or death from self-harm were unconstitutional, will continue to be litigated in court. Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw and Consuelo Callahan said in the majority opinion that Seyb’s argument for a constitutional right to abortion as a health-saving measure or in cases of risk of self-harm were unlikely to align with the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which overturned Roe v. Wade. “We think it unlikely that Dr. Seyb will be able to square the district court’s perspective on the history and tradition concerning abortions with the Supreme Court’s perspective in Dobbs,” the majority decision said. “… Idaho has a strong interest in limiting abortions to those allowed under its law. This interest clearly outweighs the potential harm to Dr. Seyb of having to abide by Idaho’s law pending the resolution of this appeal.” Wardlaw concurred with the majority decision. Judge Marsha S. Berzon disagreed, writing that the high court’s decision only applied to elective abortions, and not when the procedure may be medically necessary or indicated. Berzon agreed with district court Judge B. Lynn Winmill, whose previous order argued there was likely a “fundamental right” to abortions to preserve the mother’s health. Berzon also argued that the risk of harm for Seyb’s patients was greater than that of the state’s. “… with the stay imposed by the majority in place, some women with serious pregnancy complications will during the pendency of this appeal be required to continue their pregnancies at serious, permanent risk to their health,” Berzon wrote. “The risk, absent the injunction, to Dr. Seyb’s pregnant patients of serious and lasting harm short of death is definitionally a risk of irreparable injury.” Seyb said in a written statement, “Laws that criminalize abortion make pregnancy less safe.” “I will continue to advocate for the right of every patient to make important medical decisions without government interference,” he said. The conservative Christian advocacy group the Idaho Family Policy Center, which helped author Idaho’s abortion ban allowing civil lawsuits against doctors, celebrated Friday’s decision in a press release. “Pregnant mothers don’t have a constitutional right to abortion merely because they threaten to harm themselves,” Idaho Family Policy Center Blaine Conzatti said in the release. “Women in mental health crises need treatment, not abortion. This decision ensures that our pro-life laws here in Idaho will continue protecting both mother and baby.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.body: In a rare but legally required move, the Canyon County Board of County Commissioners on Thursday appointed naturopathic medical doctor Brett Butterfield to fill a vacancy on the Vallivue school board. If a school board in Idaho fails to fill a vacancy within 120 days, the local county commissioners are required to make the appointment. Trustee Toni Brinegar resigned on June 9, which was 142 days ago as of Thursday. “This is a statutory requirement,” Canyon County Chief Civil Deputy Aaron Bazzoli told the commissioners at Thursday’s meeting. He said the school district provided Butterfield’s name, but there were “some issues with how they went about the process.” Commissioner Leslie Van Beek thanked Bazzoli for putting on the record the county’s statutory authority to make the appointment. “I don’t know that the board has been asked — not in my tenure — to be the one that appoints a person for a vacancy on a school board,” she said. She then made a motion to appoint Butterfield. “We’re not here to overstep the wishes of the Vallivue school board,” Van Beek said. “For whatever reason, they had problems, so this was the name that surfaced as the candidate they wanted to fill that seat and I am in favor.” With the appointment secured, the five-member Vallivue school board is now back to full strength after two resignations this summer. items.body: The Snake River flows alongside the Idaho Falls greenbelt. (Photo courtesy of Hyo Lee/U.S. Department of Energy) Throughout history there has been one thing all Idahoans agreed on — water is the lifeblood of Idaho. Water has made our southern Idaho sagebrush country bloom with farms and ranches, and water has been crucial for the protection of our wildlife and our outdoor way of life. Protecting Idaho’s water rights from outside threats has been an article of faith — almost a religion — and any attempt by outsiders to get their hands on our water has been fighting words for all Idaho politicians regardless of political party or persuasion. Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights That’s why the Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming “supremacy” over Idaho’s water serving the Idaho National Laboratory is a gut punch to the people of Idaho. But our current political leaders, unlike those throughout history, have played a role in giving the Trump administration the notion that Idaho is a lap dog for whatever the president wants by their silence and eagerness to partner with the federal government regardless of the consequences for Idahoans, their economy and their way of life. Last summer, without informing the people of Idaho, Gov. Brad Little signed a memorandum of understanding with the Trump administration hoping that the Idaho National Laboratory could become a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and accept 33 percent of all radioactive waste generated in the country . Little has not explained how this campus and taking the waste will affect our precious water supply nor how it will impact the Snake River Aquifer, which supplies a significant amount of water to our southern Idaho farms, ranches, trout farms and cities. Other than a few comments for a story published by the Idaho Capital Sun , the governor has said little about how this major initiative will affect Idaho. Our congressional delegation has also remained silent on this issue except to say the campus will bring economic prosperity and jobs to eastern Idaho. Now, through the lawsuit the Trump administration has filed in U.S. District Court, we know that the federal government views the water it receives from Idaho as its water and that Idaho has no legal right to curtail water to INL even during one of the worse drought seasons in the state’s history. The Trump administration argues that federal installations like INL are “shielded by the supremacy clause” from state regulations unless “Congress has provided clear and unambiguous authorization for such regulation.” The Trump administration also argues, as it has while promoting the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and the radioactive waste repository, that Idaho’s decision to curtail INL’s water has “safety, economic and energy consequences.” Moreover, the Trump administration says that “curtailment of INL’s water right would disrupt this national nuclear energy momentum,” another way of saying it would disrupt President Trump’s quest to build nuclear reactors across the country. (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) One Boise State. Five priorities. David Hahn formally began his presidency Thursday afternoon — with a call for “shared purpose” and an outline of commitments to the Boise State University community and the state. Hahn’s list of priorities includes an ambitious fundraising drive, and enhanced partnerships with Idaho employers. “One Boise State begins with our students, faculty, and staff,” Hahn said at a ceremony marking his investiture as Boise State’s eighth president. “But it extends far beyond campus.” A president’s investiture is steeped in academic tradition, and Hahn’s ceremony was steeped in Bronco culture — with performances by a Boise State choral ensemble and the Blue Thunder Marching Band, and an unannounced cameo from football coach Spencer Danielson. Thursday’s ceremony also came nearly four months into Hahn’s actual presidency; the State Board of Education hired Hahn on July 1 , bringing a turbulent 16-month job search to a conclusion. But Hahn leveraged the moment, and used a 17-minute speech, to hammer home the “one Boise State” theme. He also articulated his five goals: student success; preparing graduates for the workforce; university research; philanthropy and athletics. Hahn’s to-do list contained at least one new wrinkle. He pledged to build on Boise State’s $500 million Unbridled fundraising campaign, setting a new $700 million target with an emphasis on student opportunities, research and endowed dean’s positions. “We can do that, together,” he said. Boise State hit the $500 million target in 2025 , and Unbridled has now raised $565 million. Hahn — who came to Boise State from the University of Arizona, where he served as dean of the college of engineering — restated his commitment to research. He again pledged to pursue top-tier R1 research status through the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education, a designation that could bring more research funding to the university. He also said Boise State should put its research to work “to power and protect” Idaho. Hahn also said Boise State needs to work closely with Idaho businesses from high-tech to healthcare, with a focus on hands-on learning and internships. “Our responsibility is to prepare the next generation of talent.” Hahn doubled down on athletics. Weeks after the State Board of Education gave Boise State athletics the go-ahead to run on an $18 million deficit — and use other university funds to make up the gap — Hahn called sports an essential part of the university’s mission. Hahn said Boise State can build one of the nation’s premier athletic programs, even in a turbulent time for intercollegiate sports . “Boise State will not sit on the sidelines and wait for someone else to determine our future,” Hahn said. But Hahn said his first commitment — and his highest priority — is student success. And Hahn began his speech with a shoutout to the ceremony’s opening speaker: Ramiro Mendoza, a Boise State junior majoring in marketing. items.title: Chrissy Teigen joins Idaho women who needed abortions in final push for ballot initiative
items.summary: Chrissy Teigen, a former model and business owner, sits next to Melanie Folwell, lead organizer of the ballot initiative campaign, at Neckar Coffee in Boise, Idaho, as part of a final push to pass the ballot measure on Election Day. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families) It took two years for Chrissy Teigen to realize she’d had an abortion and not a miscarriage, longer to
items.body: Chrissy Teigen, a former model and business owner, sits next to Melanie Folwell, lead organizer of the ballot initiative campaign, at Neckar Coffee in Boise, Idaho, as part of a final push to pass the ballot measure on Election Day. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families) It took two years for Chrissy Teigen to realize she’d had an abortion and not a miscarriage, longer to understand what went wrong in her pregnancy, and not until this week to realize she hadn’t fully grappled with it emotionally. Teigen, a former model and business owner, came to Idaho on Wednesday to make a final push leading up to Nov. 3 in favor of Proposition 1, the ballot measure that would restore access to abortion in Idaho. The state has a near-total ban that applies to any stage of pregnancy, with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life. The initiative, if passed, would also protect access to birth control and fertility assistance treatments such as in vitro fertilization. Opponents to the measure have called the initiative too extreme because it would allow abortions up to fetal viability, which was the law in Idaho prior to the ban, with exceptions after that point when the pregnancy threatens a patient’s health or life. Prior to a rally in downtown Boise with Prop 1 volunteers and supporters, Teigen — who lived in Idaho Falls in the early 1990s — met privately at a coffee shop with 12 Idaho women who have been telling their stories for the campaign about needing abortion care in Idaho. The women sat in a circle and told brief versions of their stories: miscarriages that led to septic infections because of hesitant medical providers, travel out of state for fatal anomalies and catastrophic health complications, and memorials to the babies they lost. Nonprofit organization Idahoans United for Women and Families, which has led the campaign for the initiative, coordinated the event, and owners of Neckar Coffee donated the space and coffee. Kate Campbell spoke of her son, Remy, and the infected placenta that caused her water to break at 20 weeks and begin labor. A fetus generally can’t survive outside of the womb before 22 weeks, and every day that goes by without an abortion procedure increases the risk of a potentially life-threatening infection, which can cause organ damage and lead to fertility loss. Since Idaho’s law only allows for intervention to save a patient’s life, doctors decided not to wait until she was close to death and airlifted Campbell to Utah for care. Utah allows abortion until 18 weeks, and after that, the law includes an exception to preserve a patient’s health, not just to prevent death. “The only ‘cure,’ if you will, for an infected placenta is giving birth,” Campbell said through tears. She now has a 14-month-old daughter. Rebecca Crozier and other Idaho women sit side-by-side across from Chrissy Teigen to tell their stories of needing abortion care and being unable to access it in their home state because of the near-total ban. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families) Desi Ballis had a similar story about a virus she contracted early in pregnancy that caused a fatal anomaly that also put her health in danger. A doctor at her 20-week ultrasound told her she needed to get to Utah as quickly as possible, and she and her husband, Morgan, made the five-hour drive and called multiple hospitals and clinics before they found someone who could help. “It was just horrific,” Ballis said. Others included Rebecca Crozier, who received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly at 11 weeks and told Stateline her story this week, and Abby Nichols , who traveled to Seattle for an abortion after she received a fetal diagnosis of Trisomy 18, a chromosomal abnormality that is often fatal or life-limiting. items.body: If you distrust government with spending and tax decisions, why would you put politicians at your state capitol in charge of more of it? That’s the question at the center of Idaho’s current debate over property taxes. There is no statewide property tax in Idaho, but local governments can collect property tax revenue. Property taxes frustrate homeowners for understandable reasons. Paying off your mortgage does not end the annual bill. A rising home value does not put cash in your checking account. For retirees and families with tight budgets, the burden can be substantial. But property taxes in Idaho are a creature of local government: schools, fire departments, cities, sewer, etc. In many cases, local voters have approved the new taxes and fees collected. If you’ve voted in favor of a bond, levy, or other local tax measure, you are partly responsible for the extra rate you might be paying. There are various ideas on how to eliminate the local property tax burden, but all of them have drawbacks. For example, we examined the concept of doing away with property taxes and, in exchange, giving local governments the option to adopt limited sales taxes. The concept is that this spreads the burden and allows visitors to cover part of the burden. It might work well in some areas but would likely be a burden too heavy to handle in others. It wasn’t a proposal; it was a thought experiment. Others have suggested you can do away with local property taxes by simply having local governments be funded by the state in Boise. In other words, they want state taxpayers to pay for local government decisions. But directing state revenue toward local property tax replacement creates two significant trade-offs: greater dependence on Boise and less room for other state tax reductions (such as the income tax). Today, local elected officials must answer to local voters for their spending and many of the taxes supporting it. The connection is imperfect, but important: Officials who approve spending should face the taxpayers expected to finance it. Under a state-funded replacement system, local officials would increasingly look to the Legislature for revenue. Instead of having to justify spending to local taxpayers, they would lobby for larger distributions from Boise. Local budgets would become more dependent on legislative formulas, negotiations, and priorities. Supporters argue that local control would survive because local officials would still decide how to spend the money. But spending authority is only part of the equation. Whoever controls the funding holds considerable power over the recipient. Future legislatures could also change it. During a downturn, lawmakers would face competing demands from state programs and local governments counting on replacement dollars. Imagine a scenario where your local government leaders are not talking to you about local spending but instead wandering the halls of the state capitol looking for revenue from legislative leaders. That’s a concentration of power that is anything but conservative. We should also carefully examine what this idea would mean for future state tax cuts. After all, the state currently collects income and sales tax revenues. If some of those revenues now have to be used for local government spending, we would likely see fewer, if any, income or sales tax cuts. The dreams some have of a grocery tax abolishment would likely go out the window. This is not to say there are not viable paths forward. Idaho can and should restrain local spending, examine overlapping taxing districts, and adopt Truth in Taxation so officials must clearly disclose and defend proposed property tax increases. Communities could also be allowed to consider voter-approved exchanges of property taxes for local sales taxes. Our study shows that approach would be more feasible in some counties than others. Any exchange should include reasonable rate limits and permanent, dollar-for-dollar reductions in property tax authority

(Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Trump administration is sending election monitors to Idaho’s largest county on Election Day next week, the state’s top election official confirmed Wednesday. The decision comes as the Justice Department plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors — who the DOJ says are meant to assess local compliance with federal voting rights laws — to all 50 states. That would make for a significantly expanded presence than under the Biden administration, which sent election monitors to 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections, States Newsroom reported. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, an elected Republican, said the U.S. Justice Department notified him and the Ada County Clerk’s Office, which runs the election locally, that there will be two teams in Ada County on Election Day. Ada County Clerk Trent Tripple, also a Republican, said around six election monitors who are local to Idaho will be stationed near polling places — but not inside. In a statement, the Justice Department said its election monitors in Idaho and elsewhere will be “doing the routine election monitoring the department has done for decades.” “All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process. Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate,” a spokesperson for the federal agency told the Idaho Capital Sun. At 11 weeks, she received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly, and had to travel out of state to terminate the pregnancy because of her state’s near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Stateline) MERIDIAN, Idaho — It didn’t take long for doctors to see that something was amiss with Rebecca Crozier’s pregnancy. At her eight-week ultrasound in 2025, they mentioned a possible neural tube defect, she said, but after some research, she thought it was something that could be managed or treated. “If it was a fixable problem, I was ready to quit my job and full-time care for a disabled child,” said Crozier, who is now 27. “That was something that we were prepared to do.” In the time between the two ultrasounds, she had a dream that she was carrying a baby girl, and she and her husband named her Haven. The couple lived in eastern Idaho at the time, and drove two hours to the Boise area to see the maternal-fetal medicine specialists at St. Luke’s, the state’s largest health system. Now at 11 weeks’ gestation, the specialists told her Haven had anencephaly, which occurs when the brain does not develop normally and the skull is left open, exposing brain tissue to amniotic fluid that causes the tissue to dissolve. It is a fatal condition. Rebecca Crozier takes a photo of her belly during her pregnancy before she and her husband, Kris, were told that the fetus would not survive. (Courtesy of Rebecca Crozier) “She was missing a lot of brain tissue,” Crozier recalled. “They were very clear that this baby will not go home with you. You will not take this baby home. This baby will die in the hospital if the baby survives that long.” In many states, even ones with abortion bans, Crozier would have had the option to terminate the pregnancy. But Idaho’s near-total prohibition includes no exceptions for fatal anomalies. It’s one of 11 states that do not have exceptions for anencephaly or other fatal anomalies. Next Tuesday, Idahoans will vote to determine whether the state’s near-total abortion ban should remain the law. Proposition 1, the title of the citizen-led ballot measure, would restore access to abortion until fetal viability, which was the state law before the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. Idaho is the only state this election cycle with an initiative that would restore access in a state with a ban. In Missouri, voters will consider a different initiative — to reinstate a near-total ban after passing a constitutional amendment in 2024 allowing abortion access until viability. If Idaho’s measure passes, patients like Crozier would no longer have to leave the state for an abortion. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the rate of anencephaly among newborns is about 1 in 10,000, and those babies die within a few hours or days. Most cases end in miscarriage or stillbirth; the fatal birth defect affects about 1 in 1,000 pregnancies. Crozier’s was among them. The state of Idaho has awarded $186 million in federal rural healthcare grants — with more than $20 million going into education-related programs. On Wednesday — three days before the feds’ deadline — state officials announced that the first-year grant process was a wrap. “I’m proud of the work that brought us to this point, and I’m excited to see these investments improve care for Idaho families across our state,” said Sen. Julie VanOrden, R-Pingree, the co-chair of a legislative oversight committee that has reviewed the grant applications. Year One: Some highlights The two biggest education-related awards have been in the works for some time . About $12.5 million will go into a suite of 11 initiatives to encourage rural students to pursue healthcare careers. Most of these programs are co-ops involving multiple colleges and universities. The biggest of the group is a $4.3 million Boise State University-led mobile simulation lab project, designed to bring clinical training into rural communities. The State Board of Education will receive $8 million for graduate medical education — rural fellowships and residencies for medical school graduates. Here’s a look at some other education-related grants: The University of Idaho will receive $2 million to create a statewide chronic disease education network. Idaho State University will receive $2 million for a cognitive care pathway network. The U of I and Eat Smart Idaho will share nearly $1.6 million for chronic disease prevention and cancer screening programs. Another U of I grant, of close to $1.2 million, will go toward a pediatric psychiatric assistance line and mental and behavioral health programs. Idaho Educational Services for the Deaf and the Blind will receive nearly $900,000 for a mobile pediatric clinic, which will provide specialized hearing testing in rural Idaho. “For many Idaho families — especially in rural areas — affordable, accessible health care is a real concern,” Gov. Brad Little said in a news release touting the first-year grants. “This investment recognizes those challenges and puts resources where they’re needed most.” Year Two funding: No news yet There was some considerable confusion Wednesday about Idaho’s second-year grant. On Wednesday, as state officials announced the wrapup of their first-year grant program, the Trump administration issued a news release that at least implied an additional $186 million was on its way. “Today, the Trump Administration announced nearly $186 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to improve healthcare access across rural Idaho,” the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services news release said. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) How competitive is the race to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate? It depends which poll you look at. According to a poll released last week by the campaign for Todd Achilles, an independent running for U.S. Senate, Republican incumbent Jim Risch has only a six-point lead over Achilles. Eight percent of voters were undecided, the poll found. The poll buoyed a claim by the Achilles campaign: Victory could be within reach. State Rep. Todd Achilles speaks from the House floor on the morning of March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “That tight margin confirms what we’re hearing in every corner of Idaho: voters are tired of career politicians controlled by their party bosses,” Achilles, 58, said in a statement with the poll’s release on Oct. 23. But the latest poll didn’t ask about support for the other two candidates in the race, which has drawn one of the most active attempts in years at unseating Risch, 83, who’s seeking a fourth, six-year-term. And Risch’s campaign polling — featuring the full line up of candidates — shows him pummeling Achilles. In the run up to Election Day in a state without much independent polling, that’s the sort of divide in polling outcomes that some pollsters expect voters to see. “Usually about this time, the candidates or the campaigns for ballot issues are publishing polls that show you that they’re going to win,” Stuart Elway, a longtime independent pollster in Washington state, said in an interview. In Idaho, independent political polls — which aren’t backed by a campaign or a special interest group — are hard to come by. They would offer a different perspective, Elway said. Stuart Elway, a retired longtime independent pollster in Washington state, speaks to journalists ahead of the 2023 legislative session in Washington. (Photo courtesy of Stuart Elway) “An independent poll that’s not sponsored by any party or candidate or interest group gives you an objective measure of how the election is going, and I think more importantly, what the people are thinking about when they’re thinking about the election,” he said. Some polling experts say that Idaho lacks independent polls because the state is reliably Republican controlled, and independent pollsters aren’t willing to invest the high funds needed to conduct reliable polling. Instead, there are candidate and special interest groups polling in Idaho, like the back and forth of polls released by the campaigns of Risch and Achilles. The poll released last week by Achilles’ campaign, conducted by VoteNexus , had info on other races — including 54% opposition for Proposition 1, a ballot initiative to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban. In other key races, like for governor, and two U.S. House seats, Republicans were in the lead. items.body: An influenza vaccine is pictured at the Ellis R. Shipp Public Health Center in West Valley City on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Idaho health officials on Tuesday reported the state’s second flu death in the 2026-27 influenza season. The death was of a resident of Elmore County, a rural area outside Boise, who was in their 80s, the regional health agency, Central District Health, announced. The first death, reported last week, was of an Owyhee County man who was older than age 65. The deaths come as public health officials say that influenza is spreading earlier in the year than usual. In recent weeks, emergency department and urgent care visits related to the flu have been higher than they were during the same time last year, state health officials say. Idaho has averaged about 60 reported influenza-related deaths annually for the last five flu seasons, with most reported deaths among people over 50, according to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Officials at Central District Health say vaccination is the best way to reduce the risk of severe flu illness. “While most people who get the flu recover without serious complications, some groups are at higher risk for severe illness, hospitalization, and death,” said Dr. Jaime Butler-Dawson, the health district’s epidemiology program manager. “These include adults age 65 and older, pregnant people, young children, people with obesity, and those with weakened immune systems or chronic conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes, or kidney disease.” According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year’s vaccines are designed to protect against three different influenza viruses expected to circulate during the flu season. Symptoms of the flu include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. Although most people who get the flu recover after a few days, some can have serious complications that can lead to hospitalization or death. items.body: The College of Western Idaho says its first major fundraising campaign was a $33 million success. On Tuesday, CWI said its Powering the Treasure Valley campaign had exceeded its $30 million goal — funding capital projects and scholarships at the state’s largest community college. “This campaign has always been about our students,” CWI President Gordon Jones said in a news release Tuesday. “Every gift has helped create more opportunities for students to pursue an education, develop the skills employers need, and build a future close to home.” The campaign, launched in July 2023, will leave an imprint across CWI’s landscape. Money will go toward three capital projects on the Nampa campus: The campaign helped fund the Norco Health & Science Building and Agricultural Sciences Complex , which both opened in 2025, and the CapEd Student Success Center, a student services complex that opened earlier this year. Campaign funds will also go toward the CWI downtown Boise campus and the Micron Academic Center , which is expected to open in fall 2027. CWI says the campaign also supports student aid. Since the launch in 2023, CWI has increased its annual scholarship awards from $609,000 to more than $1 million this year. However, the completed fundraising campaign won’t support two other high-profile initiatives on CWI’s radar. This money will not go toward deferred maintenance on the recently acquired Ford Idaho Center , although college officials have said fundraising will be a component in covering the $25 million in maintenance costs. This money also will not go toward an endowment-based initiative to launch CWI’s first intercollegiate athletics programs. “When CWI launched Powering the Treasure Valley … we committed to two priorities: improving the student experience and adding capacity so we can serve more students,” college spokesman Ashley Smith said in a text Tuesday.

(Photo courtesy of the Idaho Family Policy Center) Opponents of the proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to pull TV ads paid for by the Idaho Democratic Party in favor of the initiative. The conservative, Christian advocacy organization, the Idaho Family Policy Center, and leaders with a political action committee that opposes the initiative, Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, brought the lawsuit. The ballot initiative Prop 1 would repeal Idaho’s abortion ban, allowing the procedure up to viability or after in cases of emergency, enumerate rights related to a range of reproductive healthcare, and provide legal liability protections for healthcare providers who provide that type of care. The initiative will be before Idaho voters in the Nov. 3 general election. The lawsuit, filed in Canyon County court, alleges that the supporters and authors of Prop 1, a group called Idahoans United for Women and Families, paid the Idaho Democratic Party to run ads in favor of the initiative in order to pay the more favorable rates that broadcasters are required to charge to political candidates ahead of elections. The ads were run on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens. “Pro-abortion activists cheated their way into cheaper television advertisements to stump for their radical abortion ballot initiative,” Idaho Family Policy Center President Blaine Conzatti said in a written statement. “Instead of playing by the rules of the game as outlined in our state campaign finance laws, Idahoans United for Women and Families colluded with the Idaho Democratic Party to mislead voters and gain an unfair advantage. Idaho voters deserve transparency — not shell games and dirty tricks.” Idaho Democratic Party spokesperson Avery Roberts called the lawsuit “frivolous” in an email to the Idaho Capital Sun. She said it was “another attempt by opponents of Prop 1 to distract from the devastating consequences of Idaho’s extreme abortion ban.” “Women are being forced to leave the state for lifesaving medical care, and the politicians responsible have done nothing to fix it,” Roberts said. “Instead of addressing the harm this ban has caused, opponents are trying to silence the families speaking out, even after the Secretary of State’s Office confirmed our advertising complies with Idaho campaign finance laws. We won’t be intimidated into silence. Idahoans deserve to hear these families’ stories and make up their own minds on November 3.” The family policy center helped author Idaho’s law allowing family members of an aborted fetus to sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. It has also been a supporter of Idaho’s criminal abortion ban, which includes felony prison penalties for abortion providers. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) The Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane’s office, which oversees statewide elections, told Boise State Public Radio Friday that the ads did not violate campaign finance laws. Secretary of State’s Office spokesperson Joe Parris told the Sun Monday that the office was not investigating an ad about Prop 1 paid for by the Idaho Democrats because it had not received a complaint about it. The Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act would restore abortion access “without government interference” until fetal viability, and would protect fertility treatments and other reproductive care such as contraception. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) Chrissy Teigen will be in Boise on Wednesday to campaign in favor of Proposition 1 , which would repeal Idaho’s strict abortion ban laws and provide protections for the procedure. Proposition 1, also called the Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act , also provides protections for access to birth control, in vitro fertilization and privacy in healthcare decisions. Chrissy Teigen (Photo courtesy of Chrissy Teigen) Teigen, who is a New York Times #1 bestselling cookbook author, model, entrepreneur and advocate for maternal health, will meet privately with Idaho mothers to talk with them about how the state’s abortion ban laws have affected them. She’ll then speak at a “Yes on Prop 1” rally, to be held from noon to 1 p.m. Wednesday at Treefort Music Hall, to encourage Idahoans to cast their ballots during the final days of early voting. The Treefort Music Hall is located at 722 W. Broad St. in Downtown Boise, and the rally is open to the public. Idahoans will decide the outcome of Proposition 1 during the Nov. 3 general election. It would take a simple majority of “yes” votes across the state to approve Prop 1. Under Idaho’s abortion ban laws, it is a felony to perform nearly any abortion, except to prevent the death of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors in Idaho can be sued for a minimum of $20,000 and be criminally prosecuted for performing an abortion. “In September 2020, Teigen underwent a medically necessary abortion at 20 weeks after experiencing a partial placental abruption, a serious pregnancy complication that put her health at risk,” a press release announcing Teigen’s appearance said. “The pregnancy was deeply wanted, but the baby was not expected to survive, and continuing the pregnancy posed serious risks to Teigen’s health.” Idaho’s abortion ban laws do not carve out an exception to protect a mother’s health, and instead only has an exception to prevent her death. Teigen, who lived in Idaho Falls as a teen, is married to singer and pianist John Legend. They have four children. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

(Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho lawmakers will weigh whether to fund several drug-prevention and treatment projects, totaling over $3 million, through the state’s endowment fund from tobacco lawsuit settlement money. The legislative Joint Millennium Fund Committee, which oversees the endowment, heard 10 proposals Friday for use of the settlement money, which must go toward drug and alcohol prevention. As of Sept. 30, the fund’s balance was nearly $43.5 million — however, some of the previously approved projects hadn’t yet been funded, according to Senior Budget and Policy Analyst Janica Bisharat. The committee is focused particularly on youth prevention and cessation in approving use of the fund for projects. Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, (right) chats with Sen. Jim Woodward, R-Sagle, on the Senate floor on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “I am laser-focused on prevention,” committee co-Chair Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, said Friday. “I have three deaths in my family already, and two or three more that are getting close. I’ve seen abuse. I’ve seen the problem, and as long as I have this position, I’m gonna focus on that. And that’s the focus of our group here is prevention.” The committee did not decide on its recommended projects to fund. The funding would need final approval from legislative budget writers on the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee during the legislative session, which begins in January. Here are the proposed projects lawmakers heard Friday: Recovery Idaho asks for $32,780 to create a certification process for recovery centers The nonprofit Recovery Idaho sought just under $33,000 to create a voluntary accreditation program for recovery centers statewide. Recovery centers provide treatment for drug and alcohol addiction and also often provide additional support for clients in treatment. “The problem right now is that the recovery community centers throughout the state are very well intentioned, but there’s a fair amount of variation and maybe not enough tracking of what exactly happens and what those outcomes are,” Andra Smith Hansen, a Recovery Idaho board member, told the committee members. Recovery centers provide support to adults, but many of those adults are parents, Smith Hansen said, and better outcomes for those adults can lead to better outcomes for their children. The money would be used to work with recovery centers statewide to develop standards, a process for accreditation and standardized metrics to evaluate outcomes. Foundation for the Idaho Conference on Alcohol and Drug Dependency seeks $28K to help train workforce The Idaho Conference on Alcohol and Drug Dependency has held a yearly conference for more than 40 years for behavioral healthcare workers, but participation is lagging and workers statewide aren’t always able to travel to the Treasure Valley for the conference, according to Leah Kalk, a board member of the foundation. Rep. Marco Erickson, R-Idaho Falls, makes a phone call from the House floor on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The foundation is seeking $28,000 for scholarships for healthcare workers statewide to travel to the conference and earn required continuing education credits. Rep. Marco Erickson, R-Idaho Falls, who works in youth prevention, said he’d attended the conference multiple times. “Part of going to ICADD is you get to network, and as a professional in that space, you’re learning the skills that you’re going to take back to your community,” Erickson said.
